t.5.53.1: Gazing upon the city of Laṅkā, blazing and shattered, its hosts of rākṣasas stricken with terror, the monkey Hanumān fell to reflecting.
t.5.53.2: A very great dread came over him, and self-reproach arose within him: "What is this deed that I have done in burning Laṅkā?"
t.5.53.3: Blessed are those best of men, those great-souled ones, who by their understanding restrain anger once it has arisen, as one quenches a blazing fire with water.
t.5.53.5: The very purpose for which this whole undertaking was begun has been ruined, for in burning Laṅkā I did not protect Sītā.
t.5.53.4: If this Laṅkā has indeed been burnt, then surely the noble Jānakī too has been burnt; thus by me, acting without understanding, my master's task has been destroyed.
t.5.53.7: Clearly Jānakī has perished, for no part of Laṅkā is seen unburnt; the whole city has been reduced to ashes.
t.5.53.6: This task, a slight one, had been accomplished, there is no doubt; but I, overcome by anger, have destroyed its very root.
t.5.53.8: If that task has been ruined by me through a perversion of judgment, then giving up my life right here is what seems best to me as well.
t.5.53.9: Shall I now hurl myself into the fire, or into the Vaḍavāmukha? Or shall I give my body to the creatures that dwell in the ocean?
t.5.53.10: How indeed could I, still living, look upon the lord of the monkeys, or upon those two tigers among men, I who have destroyed the very whole of the task?
t.5.53.11: Indeed, through the fault of anger, I have displayed that very fickleness of monkey-nature which is famed throughout the three worlds.
t.5.53.13: But if Sītā perishes, those two will both perish; and upon their destruction, Sugrīva together with his kinsmen will perish.
t.5.53.12: Fie upon this passionate disposition, ungoverned and unsteady, since, carried away by passion, I, though fully able, did not protect Sītā!
t.5.53.14: Having heard this very news, how will Bharata, righteous of soul and devoted to his brother, together with Śatrughna, be able to go on living?
t.5.53.16: Therefore I am bereft of good fortune, one who has lost his hold on dharma and artha, my mind seized by the fault of anger; clearly I am a destroyer of the world.
t.5.53.15: When the most righteous line of Ikṣvāku has gone to destruction, then without doubt all the people will be tormented by grief and anguish.
t.5.53.18: Or rather, that auspicious lady, lovely in every limb, protected by her own splendour, will not perish; fire does not act upon fire.
t.5.53.17: As he was thinking thus, omens appeared to him, and he reflected once more on those he had also witnessed with his own eyes before.
t.5.53.19: Indeed, fire cannot touch her, the wife of that righteous-souled one of boundless splendour, guarded as she is by her own virtue.
t.5.53.20: Surely it is through the power of Rāma and the merit of Vaidehī that this oblation-bearing fire, whose very work is burning, did not burn me.
t.5.53.22: Or rather, this imperishable lord, whose work is burning everywhere, does not burn my tail; how then will he burn the noble lady?
t.5.53.21: She who is revered as a goddess by the three brothers headed by Bharata, and who is the beloved of Rāma's heart, how could she perish?
t.5.53.23: By her austerity, her truthful speech, and her single-minded devotion to her husband, she could even burn up fire itself; fire will not burn her.
t.5.53.24: As Hanumān stood there, reflecting thus on the devī's steadfast adherence to dharma, he heard the words of the great-souled Cāraṇas.
t.5.53.25: Ah, truly a deed hard to endure has been done by Hanūmān, who repeatedly let loose a terrible fire upon the dwelling of the Rākṣasas!
t.5.53.26: This city of Laṅkā has been burned, together with its watchtowers, ramparts and gateways, and yet Jānakī has not been burned: this is a marvel indeed, a wonder to us!
t.5.53.28: Then the monkey, his heart's desire fulfilled, knowing the king's daughter to be unharmed and having seen her once more with his own eyes, resolved upon the journey back.
t.5.53.27: Through omens whose meaning was plain to see, through reasons of great weight, and through the words of the sages, Hanumān became glad at heart.
